what_its_for: Brigatinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread or cannot be removed by surgery. It works specifically in patients whose cancer has a change (mutation) in a gene called ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase). Brigatinib helps block signals that tell cancer cells to grow and divide.
how_to_take: Take brigatinib by mouth, with or without food, once a day. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, chew, or break it. Try to take it at the same time every day. If you vomit after taking your dose, do NOT take another tablet that day — just take your next dose at your regular scheduled time.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your exact dose based on your individual needs. The usual starting dose is 90 mg once daily for the first 7 days. If you tolerate it well, your doctor will likely increase your dose to 180 mg once daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 8 hours since your scheduled time, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it has been more than 8 hours, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regularly scheduled time. Never take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store brigatinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container. Protect them from light and moisture. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges while taking brigatinib, as they can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid strong medications that affect how your liver breaks down drugs — always tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medications, vitamins, and supplements you take, including herbal products like St. John's Wort. Avoid becoming pregnant or fathering a child while on this medication, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, have vision changes, or feel mentally foggy.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: new or worsening shortness of breath, cough, or fever (especially in the first week of treatment — this may be a serious lung reaction called ILD/pneumonitis); chest pain or fast or irregular heartbeat; sudden severe headache, confusion, vision changes, or seizures (signs of a brain condition called PRES); numbness, tingling, or weakness in arms or legs; unusual muscle pain, weakness, or dark-colored urine (signs of muscle breakdown called rhabdomyolysis); vision problems such as blurred vision or sensitivity to light; high blood sugar symptoms like increased thirst, frequent urination, or fruity-smelling breath; signs of high blood pressure like severe headache or dizziness; or any unusual bleeding or bruising.
when_it_works: Brigatinib does not cure cancer, but it can help slow the growth or spread of cancer cells. Some patients begin to see benefits within a few weeks, but it may take several months to know how well the medicine is working for you. Your doctor will monitor your response with regular imaging scans and tests. Keep taking the medicine as directed even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Brigatinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should use contraception during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 1 week after the last dose. Liver problems: If you have moderate to severe liver disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose. Kidney problems: Dose adjustments are generally not needed for mild to moderate kidney problems, but let your doctor know about any kidney issues. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects — report any new symptoms to your doctor promptly. Children: The safety and effectiveness of brigatinib in children has not been established.
